anchor: My mother bore me in the southern wild
title: The Little Black Boy: context
short: Published in Songs of Innocence (1789), as the campaign to abolish the British slave trade gathered force; an African child speaks of his mother's teaching.
body: The Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade was founded in London in 1787, and Wilberforce introduced his first parliamentary motion in 1789, the date on the Innocence title-page. Blake later engraved plates for J. G. Stedman's Narrative of ... the Revolted Negroes of Surinam (1796), with its images of slave torture. 'The southern wild' places the boy's birth in Africa, outside civilisation in English eyes. Erdman read the poem as a protest against slavery and racial hierarchy; later critics, including Glen, stress the poem's double vision, in which the child's consoling theology also shows the effects of a culture that has taught him to see his blackness as a lack.

sources.cite: David V. Erdman, Blake: Prophet Against Empire (Princeton, 1954; 3rd ed. 1977)

title: I am black, but oh my soul is white!
short: The line echoes the Song of Solomon 1:5, 'I am black, but comely'; the child has absorbed the equation of whiteness with goodness.
body: In the KJV the bride says 'I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem' (Song of Solomon 1:5). The boy's 'but' concedes a hierarchy even as it claims spiritual equality: his soul is 'white', the colour of purity in Christian symbolism. Erdman's text reads 'And I am black, but O! my soul is white'. The next line inverts expectations, since the English child is 'White as an angel', but the black child is 'as if bereaved of light', as though his colour were a loss. Critics differ over whether Blake endorses, ironises or simply records this language.

title: as if bereaved of light
short: 'Bereaved' means deprived, robbed: the child speaks as though blackness were a loss of light, a phrase that his mother's teaching will reinterpret.
body: The phrase 'as if' is important: he only seems bereaved. The mother's teaching in stanzas 3-5 reverses the image, since dark skin is a 'cloud' or 'shady grove' given to bear the intensity of God's love, so blackness becomes protection, not deprivation. The poem thus moves from a received racial image to a theology in which all bodies, black or white, are temporary clouds. Heather Glen notes how the child's language is shaped by what he has been taught.

title: My mother taught me underneath a tree
short: The mother teaches in the shade of a tree, facing the east; the design shows her seated with the boy, pointing to the rising sun.
body: The scene is one of natural instruction, like that of the Innocence 'Introduction' and of 'The Echoing Green', and it is set 'before the heat of day', in the cool of morning. In Blake's design for the first plate the mother sits under a tree with the boy and points towards the sunrise; on the second plate a Christ-like shepherd figure receives the two children. Keynes and Lincoln describe the plates. Facing the east, the direction of sunrise and of Eden and paradise in traditional symbolism, she offers a natural religion of the sun as God's dwelling.

title: Look on the rising sun: there God does live
short: God is located in the sun, giving light and heat to all creatures; the image combines natural religion with Psalm 19, where the sun is set in a tabernacle.
body: Psalm 19:4-6 describes God setting 'a tabernacle for the sun', which goes forth 'as a bridegroom' and from whose heat nothing is hid. The mother's teaching makes the sun God's dwelling, and his gift of light and heat a universal blessing on 'flowers and trees and beasts and men'. Some critics hear an echo of African sun-worship as reported in travel writing, others of Swedenborg, whom Blake read in 1788-9, and for whom the spiritual sun is the divine love. Either way, the theology is generous: all receive comfort and joy.

title: learn to bear the beams of love
short: Life on earth is a short schooling in bearing God's love, imagined as a heat too intense for the unprepared soul.
body: The idea that divine love can be painful, a fire that unprepared souls cannot endure, has roots in mystical writing and in Swedenborg; Blake develops it in his prophetic books too. 'A little space' is a short time. The bodies, black or white, become instruments of this education, shade against the heat; the lesson is to grow strong enough to bear God's presence. The phrase also suggests that the white child, who has less 'shade', may find the sun harder to bear, which the last stanza develops.

title: these black bodies ... Is but a cloud
short: The body is a cloud or shady grove that will vanish when the soul can bear God's heat; skin colour is temporary.
body: The singular verb ('these black bodies ... Is but a cloud') gives the line the feel of a child's grammar. The body as a cloud that vanishes recalls Pauline ideas of the earthly body as a veil to be put off (2 Corinthians 5:1-4). The 'grove' is shade from the sun, and when the cloud vanishes God will call 'Come out from the grove'. The image democratises colour, since the English boy is also in a 'white cloud' (l. 23), and both must be freed.

title: round my golden tent like lambs rejoice
short: God's 'golden tent' is the heavenly tabernacle; Isaiah 40:22 describes the heavens spread 'as a tent to dwell in'; the souls rejoice 'like lambs'.
body: The tent recalls the tabernacle of the Israelites in the wilderness and the heavenly dwelling in Isaiah 40:22 and Revelation 21:3 ('the tabernacle of God is with men'). The lambs connect the scene with 'The Lamb' and the pastoral Christ of Innocence, the Good Shepherd. In the sixth stanza, 'round the tent of God like lambs we joy', the boy repeats his mother's words, and the plate's second design shows the shepherd with the two children.

title: And be like him, and he will then love me
short: The ending is ambiguous: the black boy will shade the English boy and stroke his hair, and then be 'like him' and be loved; critics debate its irony.
body: The boy imagines a heaven where he protects the white child from God's heat, an inversion of earthly roles in which he is the stronger, more prepared soul. Yet the last line suggests he can be loved only when he is 'like him', which can be read as a hope for equality, as the residue of internalised racism, or as Blake's ironic exposure of the limits of a consoling theology. Erdman stressed the poem's anti-slavery thrust; Leader and Glen emphasise its double perspective, in which the speaker's innocence reveals more than he knows. Many teachers present the debate itself as the poem's point.
